props.title: Werner Herzog Eats His Shoe
props.initialSlug: Taste the legend, devour the truth.

sections.content: Werner Herzog's bizarre documentary short **Werner Herzog Eats His Shoe (1980)** (1980) perfectly captures the maverick director's intense dedication to filmmaking. Herzog literally devours his leather boot after losing a bet with Errol Morris, promising he'd eat his shoe if Morris completed his groundbreaking documentary Gates of Heaven (1978). The 20-minute film, directed by Les Blank, showcases Herzog cooking the shoe with garlic and herbs at Berkeley's Chez Panisse restaurant - a surreal yet deadly serious testament to Herzog's commitment to inspiring new filmmakers. This connects directly to Herzog's larger body of work like **Fitzcarraldo** (1982), where he famously hauled a 320-ton steamship over a mountain, demonstrating his extreme dedication to authentic filmmaking.

sections.content: Les Blank's documentation of Herzog's shoe consumption fits perfectly within the tradition of eccentric filmmaker portraits like **Hearts of Darkness: A Filmmaker's Apocalypse** (1991) about Coppola's troubled **Apocalypse Now** (1979) production. The short also previews Herzog's later philosophical musings in films like **Cave of Forgotten Dreams** (2010), where his distinctive narration contemplates human nature and artistic expression. Herzog's willingness to literally consume footwear speaks to the same obsessive drive that led him to film inside active volcanoes for **Into the Inferno** (2016). SUBHEAD: Herzog's Dedication to Documentary Truth

This seemingly absurd act connects to Herzog's concept of "ecstatic truth" in documentary filmmaking, which he explores more formally in **Grizzly Man** (2005) and **Encounters at the End of the World** (2007). Unlike contemporary documentarians focused purely on facts, Herzog embraces poetic truth through dramatic gestures - whether eating shoes or hypnotizing his entire cast in **Heart of Glass** (1976). The shoe-eating film, while playful, demonstrates Herzog's lifelong commitment to pushing documentary boundaries, later seen in works like **Lo and Behold, Reveries of the Connected World** (2016).
